Issued at 119 AM MST Tue Nov 24 2026

One of my favorite game shows when I was growing up was Family Feud. 
And for the weather late this Monday night, the question is, name 
something associated with Thanksgiving. And, in this case, it is 
feasting (don't know if it is the number one answer, we will 
pass to the other team). In this case, the fog monster has come
out to feast on the low level moisture in portions of the area,
mainly the Bighorn Basin as well as portions of Johnson and 
Natrona Counties. We do have a dense fog advisory out through 5 
am or 11 am depending on location. The fog should dissipate in 
Casper late tonight or tomorrow morning as a southwest wind 
increases, but may linger for longer in other locations. We will
leave the advisory as is for now, and will re-evaluate around 
expiration time (5 am).

Otherwise, things look fairly uneventful for the next two and a half 
days or so. Ridging will build over the area through Wednesday and 
bring largely quiet weather, although there could be some patchy fog 
each night. With rising thicknesses and 700 millibar temperatures, 
temperatures will once again return to above normal levels, starting 
today for some but becoming more widespread Wednesday and especially 
on Thursday, when many locations could be 10 to 15 degrees above 
normal. So, a good day to throw the football around waiting for the 
turkey to be ready. Only one other concern today will be some gusty 
wind. A passing jet streak will force some 30 knot wind at 700 
millibars to the surface, impacting the wind corridor from Muddy 
Gap to Casper. High wind is not expected, though, with the only area 
with a 1 in 2 chance of wind gusts over 40 mph on the south side of 
Casper and the higher elevations where impacts are few.

The weather then begins to turn more active Thanksgiving night as 
the next Pacific weather system begins to approach the area. There 
will be two pieces of it. The first impacts the area from late 
Thursday night into Friday. This piece be the less impactful of 
the two. This piece will mainly impact the western mountains and
bring light to locally moderate snow. Amounts do not look heavy
through this time frame. Only the mountains have a greater than
1 in 2 chance of over 3 inches of snow through Friday afternoon,
with less than a 1 in 10 chance of over 6 inches of snow. Except
for the mountains, areas East of the Divide should remain dry 
and mild with many locations into the 50s for high temperatures 
with downsloping flow.

The second, and potentially more impactful piece of the system moves 
in Friday night. However, notice the most important word in the 
previous sentence, potentially (got to love modifiers). And the X 
factor, and it is a big one, will be position of the polar jet and 
the associated cold frontal boundary with it, as it will have 
an large impact on the position, amount, intensity and type of 
precipitation. Otherwise, everything is in perfect agreement 
(note sarcasm). Some ensemble members as well some deterministic
models, like the GFS, keep the best jet forcing and cold front 
to the north. This would keep the area warmer and most of the 
precipitation over Montana, resulting in more of a glancing 
blow. Other ensemble members, along with the deterministic 
European model, bring the jet into Wyoming and drag the front 
through the area. This would bring much cooler air and more 
precipitation that could, large emphasis on the word could, 
bring the first measurable snow to the lower elevations of 
central Wyoming Saturday or Saturday night. One example of the 
difference is the 700 millibar temperatures. At 5 pm on 
Saturday, comparing the GFS to the European model, there is 
difference of 9 to 13 degree celsius difference between the 
models. Near Riverton, the GFS has plus 2 celsius, which would 
put snow levels around 9000 to 9500 feet. The European models 
has a temperature of minus 10, which would put snow levels 1500 
feet underground. So, uncertainty with the details remains very 
high. The NBM takes a middle ground, with a greater than 1 in 2 
chance of an inch or more above 6000 feet. In western Wyoming, 
many of the mountains have at least a 1 in 2 chance of 6 inches 
of snow or more in this time period. The greater than 1 in 2 
chance of a foot or more of snow is largely limited to above 
pass level though. So, we may need some highlights for this 
timeframe but I would lean more toward advisories at this time. 
A lot can change though, this is still several days out.
